title: Wonderland — Modeling Creative Strategies for Children with NLP

slides.title: What you'll see in 18 minutes
slides.headline: An idea and a method, one working demonstrator, and a plan to test it
body: The question behind the work
The model: creative roles + NLP questions
A live demonstrator
What is proven, planned and hoped
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Thank the panel. One sentence of framing: this thesis is about modeling creative strategies, and Wonderland is one way to apply them. Say plainly: this is a long-term vision with a first demonstrator, not a completed study with results.

slides.title: "That can't work"
slides.headline: The first sentence a child hears often decides whether an idea survives
body: Adults answer fast, from the best intentions
Alternative first answer: "Let's see what you imagine"
Creative thinking = generating, evaluating and improving ideas
slides.visual: Two speech bubbles side by side: 'That can't work' vs 'Let's see what you imagine'
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Quote the three adult replies from the thesis (that can't work / makes no sense / first learn how). Contrast with the Wonderland answer. Link to creative thinking as generating, evaluating, improving ideas (OECD PISA 2022, as cited). Pause. Pose the question: what helps a child keep going with an unusual idea?

slides.title: Why me — and why NLP
slides.headline: Modeling transfers a strategy, not an identity
body: Life goal: leave a better world for the next generations
Mentoring ~200 engineers: never "200 copies of myself"
NLP modeling: learn the steps, build your own way
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: In my own words: one of my life goals is to leave the planet better for those after us. As an engineer I trained about 200 engineers; the aim was never 200 copies of myself but people who find their own way and in places surpass me. That is what NLP modeling means to me, and what I want to adapt for children.

slides.title: Four research questions
slides.headline: What this thesis sets out to explore — not yet answer
body: 1. Does separating imagining from planning and checking help?
2. How can Lumi ask for clarification without taking over the idea?
3. How do 'What do you want? Why does it matter? How will you know?' shape creation?
4. Can seeing and changing a drawing make learning-by-trying easier?
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Read the four questions slowly. State scope: the thesis describes the idea, the method and possible future checks; no results on children's long-term progress exist yet, and assumptions are not presented as findings.

slides.title: Dreamer → Realist → Analyst
slides.headline: One starting point for structuring creative work — an assumption to test
body: Dreamer: imagine without early criticism (open, Milton-style invitations)
Realist: turn the idea into steps (precise, Meta Model questions)
Analyst: what is missing, what could go wrong, what to improve
Children move between roles; creation is not linear
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Present Disney roles as one starting point, not the method. Name the assumption explicitly: separating roles may help when a child gives up too early. Give the Meta Model example 'Huge compared to what?' and the Milton-style 'What if your house could travel among the clouds?' — and the thesis line: this is not hypnosis or hidden influence.

slides.title: Feedback, not failure
slides.headline: A T.O.T.E. loop where the child makes the last decision
body: Goal → attempt → re-check → continue or finish
Bridge too short? "Does it reach both towers?"
Praise the choice, not the label ("You tried three wing shapes")
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Walk the bridge example from the thesis table. Connect to logical levels in one breath: behaviour (trying), capability (setting and checking a goal), belief (mistakes are allowed), identity ('I am someone who creates'). Contrast specific praise with 'you're a genius'. Re-anchor: the child decides.

slides.title: Live: from a spoken idea to a drawing
slides.headline: What the current demonstrator does today — watch who makes each decision
body: Empty world → "Draw a car" → "Add a dog" → "Make the dog smaller"
Every change is visible; the child compares it with the idea in their head
Fallback: 60-second recording
slides.visual: Live prototype on the presentation laptop; recorded clip ready in a second tab
slides.process_notes: [time-box 2:30] [if the demo fails: 'Here is the same sequence recorded last week' — play clip, keep talking through the decisions]
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Pre-frame: watch who decides. Run the four commands. Narrate the compare step. Say explicitly what the build does today (voice changes the drawing) and what it does not yet do (Lumi's adaptive questioning is a design target).

slides.title: Illustration: how Lumi should ask
slides.headline: An imagined dialogue — the design target, not a recorded session
body: "What could the robot do?" → "How will we know the turtle is safe?"
"If you were the turtle, would anything scare you?" → "How could we make it quieter?"
The child chooses each next step
slides.visual: Dialogue panel with a visible label: ILLUSTRATIVE — not a real session
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Say first: this conversation is imagined, as stated in the thesis. Show the three perspectives (what I want / the turtle / the beach) and the ecology question. Point out that Lumi never adds ten ready-made solutions; the child decides.

slides.title: Exists · planned · hoped
slides.headline: A marathon, not a sprint
body: Exists: voice-to-drawing demonstrator
Planned: drawing and shape input, 3D, returning to your world, shared worlds
Hoped (not yet tested): Lumi adapting to each child without labels
Direction: workshops with parents and children; a physical creative space
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Walk left to right. Name each layer. Mention the parent/environment direction from my later reflection as a future direction, not part of the thesis results.

slides.title: What if not — risks and the validation ladder
slides.headline: A pretty AI drawing is not evidence of learning
body: Risk: AI takes over authorship → the child must stay the main creator
Limit: not therapy; the child can refuse, pause, stop
Ladder: adult usability → small consented pilot → independent raters → transfer without Lumi
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: State the risks without softening. Then the ladder from the thesis evaluation plan, with two indicators named aloud: child-initiated changes, and 'I changed this because…'. Add: this is not a startup pitch; it needs further study of developmental psychology and child safety.

slides.title: Help me choose the first indicators
slides.headline: Which two signals would convince you that a child — not the tool — did the creating?
body: Ideas proposed by the child
Self-initiated changes
"I changed this because…"
Transfer without Lumi
slides.speaker_notes: CUE NOTES: Close the opening loop: as a boy I watched in my grandfather's workshop how something new was made from a piece of wood. That is the experience I want to protect. Then the ask: which two of these indicators would you test first? Hand over to questions.
